title: The chip that built Intel
hook: Memory chips made your name. Now Japan makes them cheaper, and your future may be somewhere else.

profit.label: Cash
profit.hint: Money Intel has to spend today

future.label: Future
future.hint: How ready Intel is for the age of the PC

intro.text: California, 1982. You run Intel, the company that made its name with memory chips, the tiny parts that help a computer remember things. Last year IBM put another Intel chip, the 8088, inside its new personal computer. That chip is the computer's brain, and the PC is selling far better than anyone expected.

s_goal.text: Memory chips still bring in more money than anything else you make. But in Japan, makers like NEC, Hitachi and Fujitsu are making memory chips better and cheaper every year. You need money for research and new factories, and sooner or later you must decide which business is Intel's future.

d1.title: IBM wants a piece of you
d1.setup: IBM, the giant whose PC runs on your chip, offers to buy a share of Intel. The money would pay for research and new factories. But IBM would own part of Intel, and your company has always made its own decisions.
d1.question: Do you take IBM's money, and how do you use it?
d1.advisor: IBM's money would bring us closer to the PC business. But a part-owner may want a say in our choices.

options.label: Take the money and invest it in memory chips, where you still earn most today.
options.outcome: You pour IBM's money into new memory lines. For a while they run flat out, but the Japanese keep cutting prices, and each new chip sells for less than the last.
options.why: Memory was the business Japan was winning on cost. You put fresh money into the fight you were losing, not the one you could win.
options.better: Take the money, but spend it on research and the PC brain chips, where Intel led.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you spent new money defending a business where rivals made things cheaper.

options.label: Take the money for research and factories, even though IBM will own part of Intel.
options.outcome: In December 1982 IBM pays $250 million for a share of Intel, about one-eighth, and you put the money into research and more factory space. IBM is now a big buyer and a part-owner.
options.why: You got money to grow from the company that was making your chip famous, and you spent it on the future, not on the past.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you used a big customer's money to build for the future.

options.label: Say no and stay fully independent, even if you have less money to grow.
options.outcome: You keep Intel fully yours, but money is tight. New factories wait, and IBM starts to wonder whether a small, stretched supplier can keep up with its PC.
options.why: Your freedom was worth something, but you turned down money for growth just as the PC took off.
options.better: Take the money, keep control of your decisions, and spend it on research and capacity.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you chose independence over growth money just before a boom.

text.text: 1983 and 1984 are boom years, and your new memory lines run day and night. Then, late in 1984, the boom ends almost overnight. Orders vanish, and memory prices start to crash, just as your new lines are at full speed.
1983 and 1984 are boom years, but without IBM's money you can't build as fast as demand grows. Then, late in 1984, the boom ends almost overnight. Orders vanish, and memory prices start to crash.
1983 and 1984 are boom years. PCs fly off the shelves, and in 1984 Intel makes a record profit. Then, late in 1984, the boom ends almost overnight. Orders vanish, and memory prices start to crash.

d2.title: The memory price war

setup.text: Japanese makers get more working chips from each batch than American makers do, so their costs are lower and they keep cutting prices. Your new memory lines make it worse, because now you have even more chips to sell at a loss. Meanwhile the PC brain chips have quietly become your core business.

Japanese makers get more working chips from each batch than American makers do, so their costs are lower and they keep cutting prices. For five years the main memory chips have been a small part of what you sell, while the PC brain chips have become your core business. But memory is where Intel began, and many of your people still think of Intel as a memory company.

d2.question: What do you do about memory?
d2.advisor: Staying means more losses. Leaving means giving up the business that built Intel. Which cost can we live with?

options.label: Build a huge new memory factory to bring your costs down to Japan's level.
options.outcome: You start a huge new memory factory. Before it is half built, prices fall again and the Japanese are still cheaper, so you are left with a giant bill and a building you can't use.
options.why: Matching Japan on cost would take years and a fortune, in a market that was collapsing. It was the biggest bet on the weakest business.
options.better: Stop putting money into memory and move your factories to the PC brain chips.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you doubled down on a losing race during a crash.

options.label: Keep making memory chips and wait for prices to recover, even as losses grow.
options.outcome: You hold on into 1985, hoping prices will come back. They don't. A newer memory chip now sells for under $3, and Intel expects to keep losing money on them.
options.why: Waiting felt careful, but prices kept falling, and every month in memory cost money that the processors needed.
options.better: Face the numbers early, and move people and factories to the chips that were already your core.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you waited for a recovery that was never coming.

options.label: Leave memory chips now and move factories to PC chips, despite Intel's history in memory.
options.outcome: You stop making the main memory chips at the start of 1985. It hurts, and some of your oldest engineers feel betrayed, but the factories and people you free up go straight to work on PC brain chips.
options.why: You read the market early. Memory was a small, losing business, and the PC brain chips were your future.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you left a losing business before it dragged you down.

d3.title: Leave the business you started?

setup.text: Your half-built memory factory is losing money every day. Japan now makes most of the world's memory chips, and the main memory chips are less than 5% of your business, yet they are dragging all of Intel down.

Intel made the first big-selling memory chip back in 1970. Now Japan makes most of the world's memory chips, and the main memory chips are less than 5% of your business, yet they are dragging all of Intel down.

d3.question: Is it time to leave?
d3.advisor: Leaving the business we started may feel like failure. Staying could cost even more if we cannot win.

options.label: Stay in and ask the US government to stop Japan selling chips below cost, even if it takes years.
options.outcome: Your lawyers take the case to the US government, but rulings take time. Meanwhile every memory chip you make still loses money, and your best engineers are stuck on a losing product.
options.why: Help from the government was slow and uncertain, and it could not fix your higher costs. You stayed in the business that was draining you.
options.better: Leave the main memory chips, keep the special ones where you are strong, and fight unfair pricing on the side.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you hoped for rescue instead of changing course.

options.label: Leave the main memory chips, but keep EPROMs, special memory chips you still sell well.
options.outcome: In 1985 Intel leaves the main memory business it started. You keep the EPROMs, special memory chips that hold data even when the power is off, and accuse Japanese makers of selling them below cost. In 1986 the US trade body rules for you.
options.why: You cut the loss that was hurting you, kept a memory business where you were still strong, and freed your people for the PC brain chips.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you walked away from your first business to save the company.

options.label: Leave all memory at once, so every person and factory works on PC chips.
options.outcome: You walk away from all memory, even the special chips that still earn money. Everyone knows where Intel is going now, but you have thrown away cash you will soon need.
options.why: Leaving the main memory chips was right, but the special ones still made money in a hard year.
options.better: Leave the losing memory chips, and keep the ones that still pay their way.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you cut the good with the bad.

text.text: Late 1985. You are still making memory chips, still losing money on them, and the PC boom is over. Sales have fallen, and Intel has more factories and people than it can pay for.
Late 1985. Leaving memory early saved you some pain, but this is still a hard year. Sales have fallen with the end of the boom, and Intel has more factories and people than it can pay for.
Late 1985. You are out of memory at last, but the giant factory you started is a heavy loss. Sales have fallen, and Intel has more factories and people than it can pay for.
Late 1985. It is one of the hardest years Intel has known. Sales have fallen 16%, and the profit is almost gone. Your costs were built for a company about twice your size.

d4.title: Too big for the business you have
d4.setup: The board wants the losses to stop. Meanwhile your next PC brain chip, the 386, has been in the making since 1982, and the first test chips are now going out to computer makers. You need money to make it a success.
d4.question: How do you cut costs?
d4.advisor: Every cut hurts people who did nothing wrong. But if we cut the wrong things, there will be no Intel left to protect them.

options.label: Cut everyone's pay a little and keep every plant open, so no one loses a job.
options.outcome: People are grateful and stay. But the old plants keep eating money, and the losses drag on much longer than they should.
options.why: It was kind, but small pay cuts could not close a gap that big, and the old plants kept draining cash.
options.better: Close the older plants, but protect research and new equipment.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you cut too little to fix the problem.

options.label: Cut research spending to save jobs. The 386, your big project, is nearly done.
options.outcome: This year's numbers look better. But the teams working on the chips after the 386 shrink, and rivals start catching up on the designs that come next.
options.why: Research was the future. Cutting it to protect the present made Intel weaker just when the 386 needed a strong team behind it.
options.better: Cut older plants and jobs, but keep spending on research and new machines.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you saved today by cutting tomorrow.

options.label: Close older plants and cut jobs, but keep spending on research and new machines.
options.outcome: Over 1985 and 1986, along with pay cuts, you close eight older plants, and about 7,200 people leave Intel. It is painful. But you keep buying new equipment and raise research spending, and in two years your factories become twice as productive.
options.why: You cut what belonged to the past and protected what would build the future: research and modern factories.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you cut deep in the past and kept investing in the future.

d5.title: Share the 386 or keep it?

setup.text: The 386 is ready, though your research cuts have left a thinner team behind it. For years, big buyers have wanted a second maker for every chip, so they are never stuck if one factory fails. AMD has made your older chips this way, but Intel feels it has not got enough back in return.

The 386 has cost $100 million to build. For years, big buyers have wanted a second maker for every chip, so they are never stuck if one factory fails. AMD has made your older chips this way, but Intel feels it has not got enough back in return.

d5.question: Who gets to make the 386?
d5.advisor: Sharing makes buyers feel safer. Keeping it gives us more control and profit. Which risk matters more?

options.label: Let many companies make it, so it spreads quickly and buyers have backup suppliers.
options.outcome: Soon several companies make your chip and fight each other on price. The 386 spreads fast, but the money from your four-year bet goes to everyone.
options.why: You gave away the reward for four years of work. A price war among makers of your own chip helped everyone but Intel.
options.better: Make it yourself, and show buyers they are safe by building it in more than one of your own factories.
options.takeaway: In 1986 you gave away the one thing nobody else had.

options.label: Let AMD make it as before, giving buyers a backup while you share the profit.
options.outcome: AMD makes the 386 too. Buyers feel safe, but many of the chips sold are AMD's, and you share the reward for four years of work.
options.why: It was the usual way, but the 386 was your best chip ever, and sharing it gave a rival half the prize.
options.better: Keep the 386 to yourself, and build it in two of your own factories so buyers feel safe.
options.takeaway: In 1986 you followed an old habit after the reason for it was gone.

options.label: Make it only yourself, in two of your own factories, even if some buyers object.
options.outcome: After a heated debate inside Intel, you keep the 386 to yourself and build it in two of your own factories, so buyers know they won't be stuck. No one else sells a 386 for almost five years, until AMD's version arrives in 1991 after a long legal fight.
options.why: You kept the reward for your biggest bet, and you answered the buyers' fear with two factories instead of a rival.
options.takeaway: In 1986 you kept your best product for yourself and solved the trust problem another way.

d6.title: IBM says no

setup.text: IBM, which you turned away in 1982, is not interested in the 386. It is busy making its own version of your older chip. Without IBM, who will build the first 386 computer?
IBM, your biggest buyer, is not interested in the 386. It is busy making its own version of your older chip. Without IBM, who will build the first 386 computer?

d6.question: How do you launch the 386?
d6.advisor: Every PC so far has followed IBM's lead. Moving without IBM could open the market, or upset your biggest buyer.

options.label: Wait for IBM. Every big PC so far has followed IBM's lead.
options.outcome: Months pass while IBM works on its own plans. Your newest chip waits on the shelf, and the money you spent building it earns nothing.
options.why: IBM had its own reasons to go slow. Waiting for your biggest buyer let it decide when your best chip could start earning.
options.better: Find a partner that wants to move first, and launch without IBM.
options.takeaway: In 1986 you waited for permission from a customer who did not want your product.

options.label: Work with Compaq, a young PC maker, and Microsoft on the first 386 PC, without IBM.
options.outcome: You, Compaq and Microsoft work together, and on 9 September 1986 Compaq announces the first PC with a 386 inside. IBM's own 386 PC arrives only in July 1987, nearly a year later. For the first time, someone other than IBM has moved the PC forward.
options.why: You stopped waiting for permission. A hungry partner got your chip to buyers fast, and the PC world learned it no longer had to follow IBM.
options.takeaway: In 1986 you launched with the partner who was ready, not the biggest one.

options.label: Sell the 386 to any PC maker, without choosing one partner to launch first.
options.outcome: PC makers buy the 386 slowly, each waiting to see what the others will do. It sells, but it takes much longer to catch on.
options.why: Without a partner to go first, everyone waited for everyone else, and your best chip caught on slowly.
options.better: Pick one eager PC maker and help it launch the first 386 computer.
options.takeaway: In 1986 you waited for the market instead of leading it.

legend.title: From memory maker to chip king

text.text: In 1986 Intel still loses money. But the 386 sells faster than Intel can make it, and by late 1987 it expects a record profit. By 1992 Intel makes 8 in every 10 computer brain chips sold and earns more than $1 billion a year. The memory company has become the PC chip company.
Because you left memory early, you lost less and moved faster. The 386 sells faster than you can make it, and Intel becomes the company whose chips are inside most of the world's PCs.
You let go of memory and bet on the PC brain chips at the right time. The 386 sells faster than you can make it, and Intel becomes the company whose chips are inside most of the world's PCs.
Intel survives the memory crash and still makes good chips. But many companies now make your 386, and the price war means Intel never earns what its best chip was worth.
Intel survives the memory crash and still makes good chips. But AMD sells the 386 too, and it takes a big part of the market you could have owned.
Intel survives the memory crash and still makes good chips. But you moved too slowly in places, and others take a big part of the PC chip market you could have owned.
You held on to memory for too long. The losses ate the money the PC chips needed, and Intel ends up as one more chip maker beaten by cheaper rivals.
Old habits and slow moves cost you the PC era. The losses ate the money the new chips needed, and Intel ends up as one more chip maker beaten by cheaper rivals.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: The board has seen enough. After three costly calls in the worst crash Intel has known, it asks someone else to lead the company.

realHistory: Intel began as a memory company, and in 1970 it made one of the first memory chips sold to the public. In the early 1980s Japanese makers made memory chips better and cheaper. In 1982 IBM paid $250 million for 12% of Intel. Intel stayed in the main memory chip business until 1985, then left it. Over 1985 and 1986 it closed eight plants and cut 7,200 jobs, and it lost $173 million in 1986. It kept its new 386 chip, a computer's brain, to itself instead of sharing it with AMD, and Compaq launched the first 386 PC in September 1986. By 1992 Intel had 83% of the market for these brain chips.
